segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the greatest novels in the English language.
Over the course of this series, we'll be moving through Dickens chapter by chapter — the fog, the lawsuit, the secrets, the deaths.
We'll ask what makes Bleak House so astonishing, and why, more than a century and a half after its first appearance, it still feels so uncomfortably alive.
To do that, I have three remarkable guests with me.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished Dickens critics of his generation.
Edmund reads Bleak House as a novel about moral character — about what it costs to be good in a world determined to wear goodness down.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who has spent his career studying Victorian institutions — and who knows more about the real Court of Chancery than perhaps anyone alive.
James brings the world that Dickens was writing into — and asks whether the novel's rage is justified.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since.
Caroline is our guide to the experience of reading — what makes you laugh, what stops your breath, what sends you back to re-read a sentence at midnight.
We begin where Dickens begins — in the fog.
The very first chapter of Bleak House opens with one of the most famous passages in Victorian fiction — and I'd like to hear from each of you about what that opening does, and why it matters.
The thing about that opening is that it arrives like weather — before you have any bearings at all.
You haven't met a character, you don't know what kind of novel this is, and Dickens simply starts:
"London. Michaelmas Term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall. Implacable November weather."
Three fragments — not even full sentences — and the whole atmosphere is there.
That word "implacable" does everything.
It isn't just bad weather — it's weather that cannot be reasoned with, that has no mercy in it.
And then the fog comes — and it keeps coming, in wave after wave of those extraordinary sentences.
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
"Defiled" — that's a moral word, lodged inside a description of geography.
Dickens is already doing something far more than setting a scene.
Caroline is right to notice the moral vocabulary — though I might frame the achievement rather differently.
What Dickens has written in that first chapter is not a political manifesto dressed in weather.
It is a superb act of literary creation — the establishment of a world with its own atmosphere, its own governing spirit.
The fog is fog — thick, particular, brilliantly rendered.
But it is also, in the highest Johnsonian sense, a general truth about human condition — the truth that we very often cannot see clearly what is right in front of us.
Consider what Dickens does when the fog reaches the Court of Chancery itself.
"At the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor in his High Court of Chancery."
"Heart" — not periphery, not symbol, but the actual beating centre.
The institution sits inside the fog as a thing of nature — not an aberration but an organ of it.
That is a greater literary achievement than any satirical tract.
Edmund's reading is beautiful, and I won't quarrel with the literary achievement — but I think we should be careful not to aestheticise the fog into pure metaphor.
The fog in the opening of Bleak House is doing something historically specific.
Dickens was writing in 1851 and 1852, and the Court of Chancery he describes was entirely real — a system of equity jurisdiction so backlogged and so opaque that cases routinely ran for decades.
The fog isn't just a governing metaphor — it's an accurate account of epistemic conditions inside that court.
Nobody knew the state of a case; nobody could tell you when it would be resolved.
Dickens had experienced this directly — his own case, in Chancery, over the plagiarism of A Christmas Carol, had cost him more in legal fees than he recovered in damages.
So when he writes —
"Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on. This scarecrow of a suit has, in course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means."
That is not hyperbole.
That is close, if anything understated, reportage.
What strikes me, listening to both of you, is that Dickens somehow manages to be all of these things at once — the literary artist, the social witness, the moralist.
And the fog is the perfect vehicle for that because fog doesn't announce its intentions — it simply is.
What I love is that the opening also has this extraordinary wit to it, which doesn't always get mentioned.
The fog creeping into the eyes and throats of ancient Chancellors, gas looming through the fog as halos — Dickens is having a dark, gleeful time.
There's a line I keep coming back to, about the mud —

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A dinosaur in Holborn Hill — the image is absurd and it's perfect.
Because the suggestion is that this world is primordial — that London hasn't evolved so much as accumulated.
The Megalosaurus is a fine example of Dickensian extravagance used with perfect control.
But I want to draw attention to what the opening does that is not merely satirical or atmospheric — and that is the introduction of the double narrative.
Dickens is the only novelist, I think, bold enough to give us two narrators of such utterly different temperament in the same novel.
The omniscient narrator of the fog chapters — cold, ironic, present tense, visionary.
And then Esther — warm, self-effacing, past tense, intimate.
The fog narrator and the hearth narrator — and between them, the whole of human experience in the novel.
That's well put — and the tense distinction matters enormously when you think about what each narrator can see.
The omniscient narrator speaks in the present tense as though the injustice is still happening — because, in a sense, it always is.
Esther speaks in the past tense because she has survived to tell the tale — she has the luxury of retrospect.
What Chancery does — what those endless suits did to real people — is strip away the possibility of retrospect entirely.
Richard Carstone never gets to look back.
Richard Carstone — and that, I think, is the perfect bridge to where we go next.
Because the fog doesn't just obscure the court — it enters people.
It gets into the lungs of the characters, as James will perhaps remind us — quite literally, in some cases.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to Chancery itself — the machine at the heart of the fog, and what it does to the people caught inside it.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Richard's Slow Unraveling: Ambition and Ruin

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast where we take our time with one of the great novels in the English language.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most painful trajectories — the ruin of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins as one of the most naturally charming young men in all of Dickens — warm, handsome, full of promise.
And yet Jarndyce and Jarndyce hollows him out, slowly and terribly, until there is almost nothing left.
With me today are Sir Edmund Leigh, who will remind us that Richard's tragedy is ultimately a moral one — a failure of will, not merely of circumstance.
Professor James Blackstone, who will situate Richard inside the actual machinery of Chancery and what it did to real people.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who I suspect will have strong feelings about whether Richard deserves our sympathy, our frustration, or both.
Let's begin with Richard as Dickens first gives him to us — and ask what exactly is lost.
The thing one must say about Richard at the outset is that Dickens gives him every advantage — save one.
He has intelligence, he has warmth, he has the genuine affection of John Jarndyce — a man not easily moved to affection.
What he lacks is the capacity to anchor himself to anything that does not float.
Dickens diagnoses this with characteristic precision early on, when Jarndyce tells Esther — and I think the phrasing is quite exact —
"The system! I am told, on all hands, it's the system. I mustn't look to individuals. It's the system."
Jarndyce speaks those words with contempt, of course — contempt for the evasion of personal responsibility that the system permits.
And that is precisely what Richard learns to do: blame the system, invest in the system, and be consumed by the system.
The tragedy is not that the court destroys him from without — it is that Richard allows it to colonise his imagination from within.
I think Edmund is right about the moral architecture, but I'd want to push back gently on the word 'allows.'
The Court of Chancery in the mid-nineteenth century was not a metaphor — it was a functioning catastrophe.
Cases genuinely ran for decades. Real families were consumed. The legal fees devoured the estates the suits were meant to protect.
There's a real case — the Jennens estate — that ran from 1798 well into the 1830s and may have inspired Dickens directly.
So when Richard calculates that the suit will come right and he need not settle to any profession — that is not mere weakness of character.
It is a rational response, in a perverse way, to a system that dangled enormous sums and had no shame about the dangling.
Dickens captures this with that devastating line about the suit — something to the effect that it has become Richard's blood and breath.
"The uncertainties and delays of this suit have become the realities of his existence."
That is Chancery's true violence — it doesn't just waste your time, it displaces reality itself.
What breaks my heart every time — and I mean every single time I've read this — is that Richard knows.
There are moments, especially early on, when he sees himself clearly and is ashamed of what he sees.
He tells Esther — and this is in one of those late-night conversations that Dickens does so beautifully —
"I know I am not steady. I know I don't do what I mean to do. I could wish to have someone near me who would help me to be steadier."
He's asking for Ada. He's asking for love to save him from himself.
And the terrible irony is that Ada does love him — completely, selflessly — and it is not enough.
Nothing is enough, because the gap inside Richard isn't loneliness — it's a refusal to be present to his own life.
Caroline puts her finger on something essential — and I think it connects to Dickens's use of the professional restlessness as a structural device.
Richard tries medicine, law, the army — each with that same initial burst of enthusiasm that Esther watches with such tender, helpless concern.
Esther's narration is at its most affecting here — she never says outright that she sees him failing, but the pity is unmistakable.
There's a moment where she reflects on his face — how it has changed — and she notes, with that controlled Estherian understatement —
"He looked like a haunted man who was always sad; always striving for something he could not find."
A haunted man. Not a wicked man. Not even a foolish man, exactly. A haunted one.
That distinction matters enormously for how we read Dickens's moral judgment — which is, I believe, one of compassion, not condemnation.
The career-hopping is worth pausing on for a moment, because it has a very specific social texture in the 1840s and 50s.
Medicine, law, the purchase of an army commission — these are the exact three professions open to a gentleman of no particular fortune and uncertain prospects.
And each one requires precisely the long-term commitment and deferred gratification that Jarndyce-and-Jarndyce has trained Richard to be incapable of.
The suit has, in a very literal sense, made him unemployable — not because he lacks talent but because it has destroyed his relationship with the future.
And then there's Vholes — and if we're talking about Richard's ruin, we cannot leave Vholes out.
Dickens gives us the definitive portrait of the legal predator — a man who presents himself as Richard's devoted servant while feeding on him steadily.
The description of Vholes is one of Dickens's great savage passages — he says Vholes is a man who —
"never smiles; who is always quietly absorbing into himself the weaknesses and misfortunes of his client."
Absorbing. It's a vampire's metabolism, dressed in legal black.
Vholes makes me furious every time — which is exactly what Dickens intends.
But I want to stay with the personal cost to Ada for a moment, because I think she's sometimes overlooked in discussions of Richard's ruin.
She marries him secretly, she uses her own inheritance to feed his obsession, she watches him die.
And Dickens gives her almost no interiority in those final chapters — we see it all through Esther's eyes, which is almost unbearably restrained.
The moment that destroys me is the deathbed scene — Richard's return to himself at the last.
"I will begin the world" — those are almost his last words — "I will begin the world."
He says it twice. He means it. And it is too late.
That is Dickens at his most merciless — not the death itself, but the clarity that arrives only at the end.
"I will begin the world" — one of the most affecting phrases in English fiction, I've long thought.
What gives it that quality is not pathos alone but the grammatical tense — the future tense, spoken from the threshold of death.
Richard has spent the entire novel refusing to inhabit the present moment — and at the end, the present moment closes.
I would argue — and this is where I part company somewhat with James's reading — that the court is the occasion of his ruin, not its cause.
The cause is a fundamental incapacity to choose — to commit to the actual over the hypothetical.
Dickens understood, as Burke understood, that character is not merely shaped by institutions — it must ultimately stand over against them.
I take Edmund's point — and I won't entirely resist it.
But I think the question Dickens is asking is more structural: what happens to a young man when a corrupt institution makes irresponsibility the path of least resistance?
Richard isn't unique — Chancery has produced dozens of Richards. That's the point of Gridley, of Miss Flite, of Tom Jarndyce before him.
Miss Flite's little birds in their cages — Hope, Joy, Youth, Peace, Rest, Life — she gives them those names because Chancery has consumed all of hers.
And then Dickens gives us the final two birds in her collection — the names she adds after Richard dies.
"The Wards in Jarndyce. And Decay. And Ruin."
Three birds. Named for what the court made of Richard, and Ada, and every other ward it ever touched.
And that image — those named birds in their little cages — brings us to the heart of what makes Richard's story so much larger than one young man's failure.
He is particular and universal at once — which is perhaps Dickens's greatest gift.
Edmund, James, Caroline — thank you for that. I think we've honoured Richard rather more than the court ever did.
After the break, we'll be turning to Esther Summerson — her narrative voice, her self-effacement, and why she remains one of the most debated characters in all of Victorian fiction.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with considerable affection.
Today we're going deep into one of the novel's most psychologically charged threads — the secret life of Lady Dedlock.
She is, on the surface, the very image of aristocratic composure — cold, remote, untouchable.
But beneath that surface lies a buried life — a love affair, a child, a history she has spent twenty years entombing.
With me today are Sir Edmund Leigh, whose moral imagination has always understood Lady Dedlock better than she understands herself.
Professor James Blackstone, who will remind us what secrecy actually cost a woman in Victorian England.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who I suspect has a great deal to say about how Dickens makes us feel Lady Dedlock's secret before he tells us what it is.
Edmund, let's begin with you — what kind of woman is Lady Dedlock, and what does her secret reveal about her character?
Lady Dedlock is, I think, one of the most genuinely tragic figures in all of Victorian fiction.
Not tragic in the operatic sense — Dickens resists that easy grandeur — but tragic in the classical sense of a noble nature brought low by a single catastrophic choice.
The choice she made — to conceal the birth of her daughter, to let the world believe the child was dead — that is the original wound from which everything else bleeds.
Dickens introduces her at Chesney Wold with that remarkable portrait of ennui — the boredom that fashionable people have raised to an art form.
He writes of her that she has beauty, pride, ambition, insolent resolve, and sense enough to portion out a legion of fine ladies.
"She has beauty, pride, ambition, insolent resolve, and sense enough to portion out a legion of fine ladies."
That word — insolent — is doing considerable work there.
It suggests not merely pride but a will that has bent the world to its purposes — and the secret is precisely the price she has paid to keep bending it.
What strikes me every time I return to those early chapters is how Dickens gives us the secret through atmosphere before he gives us the facts.
There is that extraordinary moment in chapter two when Lady Dedlock suddenly sees the handwriting on the legal documents — Nemo's handwriting — and nearly faints.
Dickens barely pauses on it.
He simply notes that she has turned ill and asks to be taken home, and then — nothing.
The reader is left holding something they can't quite name — a tremor in the narrative, a sense that the ground has shifted.
It's an almost cinematic technique — the close-up on a face trying desperately to remain composed.
And Dickens captures it with that cool, almost clinical precision he brings to moments of extreme feeling.
Yes — and I would add that Tulkinghorn registers it too.
That dreadful spider of a lawyer, sitting in his old-fashioned chambers surrounded by his secrets — he sees the crack in the mask and resolves to work at it.
Burke would have something to say about Tulkinghorn — about men who use other people's secrets as instruments of power.
But what interests me morally is this: Lady Dedlock is not without culpability.
She chose the comfort of Chesney Wold and the name of Dedlock over the acknowledgment of her daughter.
Esther lived in ignorance and in the shadow of a shame she did nothing to deserve.
That is the moral weight of the secret — not the fallen woman's disgrace, but the abandoned child's wound.
Edmund puts it very precisely — and I want to come at it from the legal and social angle, because the constraints Lady Dedlock operates under are absolutely concrete.
An illegitimate child in 1850 carried a stigma that was not merely social but legal — the child was literally filius nullius, a child of no one, with no inheritance rights and no legal identity.
For Lady Dedlock to acknowledge Esther would have been to annihilate herself — her marriage, her social position, everything Chesney Wold represents.
Dickens understood that the law didn't merely reflect social attitudes toward women — it enforced them with mechanical ferocity.
And yet — and this is what's so remarkable — he doesn't let the social machinery entirely absolve her either.
There is that terrible scene when she finally meets Esther at the brickmaker's cottage — when she takes Esther's face in her hands.
"I am your wicked and unhappy mother. Oh, try to forgive me!"
The word wicked is Lady Dedlock's own verdict on herself — and Dickens lets it stand.
That scene at the cottage is one of the most devastating in the novel — and Dickens does something very strange with Esther's narration there.
Esther tells it with such restraint — such determined composure — that the emotion becomes almost unbearable precisely because it is so controlled.
She says of her mother's face that she turned it from me, and I heard her say, in a low, trembling voice, that she durst not look at me.
"She turned her face from me. I heard her say, in a low, trembling voice, that she durst not look at me."
That phrase — durst not look — is so archaic, so almost Biblical, and it places Lady Dedlock's guilt in a register beyond ordinary social shame.
It's the guilt of one who cannot face what she has created — her own child, made strange by years of absence and silence.
And Esther, being Esther, is gentle with her.
Which is almost more than the reader can bear.
I want to bring in the figure of Nemo here — because Lady Dedlock's secret is also Captain Hawdon's secret, and the novel treats these two people very differently.
Hawdon dies in a pauper's grave in the opening chapters, his identity unknown — he is literally nobody, as his pseudonym announces.
Lady Dedlock, by contrast, has everything — status, wealth, the magnificent facade of Chesney Wold — and she has built it directly on the suppression of the very love that made her human.
Dickens was very much alive to this irony — that society rewards the successful concealment of transgression and destroys those who cannot conceal it.
Jo the crossing-sweeper and Nemo occupy the same rung of Dickens' social ladder — people made invisible by the machinery of respectability above them.
I take James's point — but I would resist the framing that makes Lady Dedlock merely a victim of social machinery.
The machinery provided the incentive — character determined what she did with it.
And Dickens is very careful, I think, to show us Lady Dedlock's secret unravelling not through any external accident but through the force of her own repressed feeling.
It is the sight of the handwriting — the involuntary response of a love she thought buried — that gives the game away.
Dickens understood — as Johnson understood — that we cannot indefinitely entomb the affections without some crack appearing.
There is something almost Greek in it — the past asserts itself through the body, through the unconscious flinch, before the will can intervene.
And then there is the ending — which I find almost insupportably moving, and which I think is Dickens at his most honest.
Lady Dedlock dies not at Chesney Wold but at the gate of the pauper's burial ground where Nemo is buried — dressed as a brickmaker's wife, anonymous, stripped of everything.
She has made herself nothing — filius nullius in reverse — to die at the side of the man and the past she could never properly mourn.
Esther describes finding her — and the prose goes very quiet, very spare.
"I passed on to the gate, and stooped down. I lifted the heavy head, put the long dank hair aside, and turned the face. And it was my mother, cold and dead."
Cold and dead.
Three words.
After all the plotting, the disguises, the slow pursuit — three words and a chapter ends.
Dickens doesn't let you sob.
He just — stops.
Cold and dead — three words that carry the whole weight of a suppressed life.
What you've all been tracing is how the secret works simultaneously on three registers — moral, social, and deeply psychological.
Edmund gives us a woman whose will has made her complicit in her own tragedy.
James shows us the iron framework of law and society that made the concealment not just tempting but rational.
And Caroline has shown us how Dickens makes us feel the secret — in the crack in the prose, in the three devastating words at the end.

In our next segment, we turn to the other great secret-keeper of Bleak House — the labyrinthine Court of Chancery itself — and ask what it means that the novel's emotional and legal mysteries are structured so similarly.

segments.title: Jo and the Margins of Society

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart — sentence by sentence, character by character — to find out what makes it endure.
I'm your host, and today we're in the company of three exceptional readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has spent a lifetime arguing that Dickens' true subject is moral character — individual souls tested by a fallen world.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows what the Court of Chancery actually was — and what it actually did to people.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House five times and still stops dead at certain sentences.
Today we're turning our attention to one of the most devastating figures in the novel — Jo, the crossing-sweeper.
A child who knows nothing, owns nothing, and is wanted by no one — except, briefly, by those who would use him.
Jo is the character who undoes me every single time, and I've tried to be prepared for it.
Dickens introduces him sweeping the mud at a street crossing near Tom-all-Alone's — which is already a name doing enormous work.
And the first thing Dickens tells us is that Jo can't read.
Not as a fact about his education, but as a kind of existential condition — signs mean nothing to him, the city is illegible.
And then Dickens asks — and this is the passage that stops me — he asks what Jo knows.
"He knows that it's hard to keep the mud off the crossing in dirty weather, and harder still to live by doing it."
That's the whole of his world — mud and the effort of clearing it, and the impossibility of living by that effort.
Dickens compounds the mud so it becomes almost a moral substance — the city's indifference made physical.
What strikes me is the precision of Dickens' rhetorical strategy in those chapters.
He is not simply asking us to pity Jo.
He is constructing an argument — that society has produced this child and then has the audacity to be offended by his existence.
There is a passage in chapter forty-seven — Jo's death — where the narrator addresses the reader with barely contained fury.
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right reverends and wrong reverends of every order."
The anaphora there — the hammering repetition of 'Dead' — is not sentiment.
It is indictment.
And even I, who resist the political reading, cannot pretend that passage is merely about one orphan boy.
Edmund's instinct is right, and the historical record makes it even more uncomfortable.
Jo is a crossing-sweeper, which was a recognised — if precarious — occupation in Victorian London.
These were children and adults who cleared horse dung and mud from street crossings in exchange for whatever a passerby might choose to drop.
It was entirely informal, entirely unprotected, and the police could move you on at any moment — which is precisely what happens to Jo throughout the novel.
'Move on' — those two words are Jo's entire legal biography.
Dickens captures it with terrible accuracy when he writes of Jo being 'constantly chivvied and moved on by the police.'
"'Move on!' Everywhere. 'Move on' — as if there were somewhere to move on to."
There was no Poor Law provision for a child with no parish of settlement, no documented origin.
Jo is not an exception — he is the system working exactly as designed.
James, that phrase — 'the system working exactly as designed' — is what Dickens is building toward, chapter by chapter.
What I find so remarkable is that Jo is also given a kind of dignity.
He is loyal to the memory of Nemo — Captain Hawdon — whom no one else mourns at all.
Nemo gives Jo a coin now and then, and speaks to him — and for Jo, that is enough to constitute a friendship.
When the inquest is held and they ask Jo what he knows of the dead man, Dickens writes it so carefully.
"He was very good to me, he was."
Five words — and they carry the whole weight of a life that received almost no kindness.
Jo doesn't have the vocabulary to eulogise.
But what he says is more piercing than any elegy.
Caroline touches on something that I think is essential and often overlooked in the more politicised discussions of Jo.
Dickens gives Jo a moral life.
He is not merely a symbol of social suffering — he exercises loyalty, he acts from something like conscience.
When Lady Dedlock comes to him in disguise — seeking Nemo's grave — Jo guides her through the streets without understanding who she is.
Dickens frames that moment with a kind of ironic solemnity — the boy who is nobody leads the great lady to the grave of the man who was her secret.
And Dickens writes — with that beautiful compressed irony — that Jo showed her the 'berryin ground' as he called it.
"The berryin ground — where they laid him as wos wery good to me."
The dialect is not condescension — it is Dickens insisting that Jo's voice, exactly as it is, carries weight enough.
And the tragedy compounds, of course, because Jo becomes a vector — he carries the disease from Tom-all-Alone's outward into respectable society.
Dickens was extremely precise about this — smallpox spreading from the slum to the drawing room.
He understood contagion in the literal sense, but the metaphor is inescapable — you cannot wall off poverty.
There is that extraordinary passage where Dickens addresses Tom-all-Alone's directly, almost as a character — warning that its 'avengers' will spread.
"There is not a drop of Tom's corrupted blood but propagates infection and contagion somewhere."
That is not metaphor for Dickens — or rather, it is both literal public health and moral argument at once.
The conditions that produce a Jo are not safely contained in the slum — they contaminate the whole social body.
And then he dies, and Dickens gives him — very deliberately — something like last rites.
Allan Woodcourt is with him, and Jo tries to say the Lord's Prayer — tries to follow Allan through it.
He has never been taught it.
Dickens writes it out — Jo repeating phrase by phrase after Allan — and it is almost unbearable to read.
"The light is come upon the dark benighted way. Dead!"
That exclamation mark after 'Dead' — it's not triumph and it's not merely sorrow.
It's Dickens refusing to let you read past it quietly.
He forces a stop.
Jo — who knows nothing, who can read nothing, who is moved on from everywhere — is given, at the last, the words of the Lord's Prayer.
And Dickens makes sure we understand that the failure to teach him those words earlier is not a private failure — it is England's.
Thank you all — that is exactly the kind of reading Jo deserves.
We'll be turning next to the question of Esther Summerson — the novel's other orphan, who survives the fog by a very different means.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been living with the fog, the Court of Chancery, and the weight of Esther's story.
But Dickens, being Dickens, refuses to let the gloom go unrelieved.
This segment we're turning to the comedy — and specifically to two figures who are genuinely, brilliantly funny, even as they unsettle us.
John Jarndyce of Bleak House — generous, self-deprecating, a little evasive — and Harold Skimpole, who may be the most dangerous comic creation in Victorian fiction.
I want to start with Jarndyce, because I think he's often underestimated as a comic figure.
His great comic mechanism — his retreat to the Growlery when things go wrong — is one of the loveliest running jokes in the novel.
He explains it to Esther with perfect seriousness.
"When I am deceived or disappointed in — the wind, and it's in the east, I take myself there, and I growl."
There's something so entirely English in that — the private room of self-managed bad temper.
But it also tells you everything about Jarndyce's relationship to his own pain: he keeps it contained, he keeps it named, and he keeps it away from the people he loves.
Quite right to start there, and I'd go further.
The Growlery is not merely a comic detail — it is a portrait of a man who has learned, at some cost, the discipline of not inflicting his suffering on others.
Burke, I think, would have recognised the type: a private stoicism that serves the social order.
And the comedy of Jarndyce's wind-vane approach to Chancery — never speaking of it directly, never naming the case — is in fact the comedy of a man who has chosen sanity over obsession.
When he says that the wind is in the east and something is going wrong with Jarndyce and Jarndyce, we laugh — but we also understand the weight behind the joke.
I'd add one thing about Jarndyce as a comic figure that I think is easy to miss.
He is genuinely funny precisely because he is genuinely good, and genuinely good people are relatively rare in satire.
His comic habit of attributing all misfortune to the wind being in the east is his way of refusing to name the real source of chaos in the novel, which is the Court of Chancery.
And as a legal historian I find that choice particularly telling — because Chancery really did do that to people.
It made otherwise rational men speak in superstitions, in weather metaphors, in anything but the plain truth of what the system had done to them.
Which brings us — with some reluctance, and yet with enormous anticipation — to Harold Skimpole.
The man who claims to be a child, accepts everyone's money, and turns charming irresponsibility into an art form.
Caroline — you've described him to me before as the most troubling laugh in English literature.
He absolutely is, and the reason is that Dickens makes him irresistible before he makes him monstrous.
The first time we meet him, he floats into the room — that's almost the word — and says something that stops you completely.
"I am a child, you know! I am a mere child. I know nothing of the art of life — nothing whatever."
And you laugh, because it's absurd — this grown man with his debts and his opinions and his excellent taste in claret.
But Dickens is doing something far more precise than simply sending up a dilettante.
He is showing us how aesthetic charm can be weaponised — how the performance of innocence can be a form of aggression.
I must say, I find myself more divided about Skimpole than most readers seem to be.
Yes, he is morally contemptible — there is no question of that by the end.
But the character is so perfectly rendered that I cannot help admiring the artistry even while deploring the man.
His defence of taking whatever is offered — Dickens gives him arguments that are almost logically coherent, which is what makes them so dangerous.
He tells Esther and the children — I am roughly quoting — that he sees no reason to resist beauty, whether it takes the form of a flower, a painting, or a five-pound note from a friend.
The equating of a flower with a debt is perfectly comic and perfectly vicious, simultaneously.
What strikes me about Skimpole from a historical angle is how precise the social portrait is.
He belongs to a very specific Victorian type — the gentleman amateur who floats on the generosity of others while treating that generosity as a natural law.
And Dickens was almost certainly drawing on Leigh Hunt — the poet and critic, friend of Keats and Shelley — which caused a tremendous scandal at the time.
Hunt was genuinely charming, genuinely talented, and genuinely dependent on his friends' purses his entire life.
What Dickens does is take the charm intact and then show you, very slowly, where its logic terminates.
It terminates with Skimpole giving up Jo's whereabouts to Bucket for a five-pound note — and then writing about it in his memoirs as a charming trifle.
That moment with Bucket is the hinge of everything, isn't it.
And what's so devastating is that Dickens has prepared us for it so meticulously.
Every laugh we've had at Skimpole's expense — every charming evasion — has been a small rehearsal for this final act of betrayal.
And then there's the passage where Esther, narrating, delivers the most controlled, most devastating sentence about him.
"I perceived that he had already begun to write about it."
That single sentence does more moral work than a chapter of denunciation.
That is the moment where Dickens' moral imagination — which, I maintain, is his central genius — operates at its most scalpel-precise.
He does not give Skimpole a villain's soliloquy.
He gives him something far worse: a complete inability to understand why what he has done could be called wrong.
That is not comedy turning dark.
That is the darkness that was always present inside the comedy, now fully visible.
And what makes the comedy survive even that revelation — what makes it so hard to classify — is that Dickens never stops letting Skimpole be funny.
Even his self-justifications are amusing.
He tells Jarndyce at one point that he has discovered he is not so much a man who owes money as a man who inspires generosity in others — a very different thing.
There's real wit there, of a kind Dickens clearly enjoyed constructing.
The problem is that the wit is precisely the alibi — the beautiful surface over the hollow centre.
There's something worth pausing on here — the question of what we're supposed to do with a character who makes us laugh and makes us complicit simultaneously.
Jarndyce and Skimpole are linked in interesting ways — both figures of generosity, one genuine, one performed.
Edmund, what do you make of the fact that Jarndyce is consistently fooled by Skimpole for so long?
It is, I think, the most sympathetically drawn flaw in Jarndyce's character — and Dickens is generous enough to make it a flaw of virtue rather than vice.
Jarndyce believes in Skimpole because Jarndyce is himself genuinely unworldly in his goodness.
He cannot quite conceive of a man who wears the costume of innocence as a calculated disguise.
There is a wonderful irony in the fact that it is Esther — not Jarndyce — who sees through Skimpole first.
The novel's moral compass is the young woman with no social power, not the wealthy philanthropist.
Esther's discomfort with Skimpole is written so subtly, and I love Dickens for that.
She never condemns him outright in her narration — she is too careful, too conscious of her own limitations.
But there are these small, precise observations — the tiny hesitations before she describes his behaviour — that tell you everything.
She says of him, at one point, that he had a freshness and a gentleness — and then she adds, very carefully, that these seemed the result of his not having any duties.
That phrase — "not having any duties" — is doing enormous work in Esther's moral vocabulary.
Esther is defined by her duties. For her, a man without duties is not a free spirit — he is a kind of absence.
And the Chancery parallel runs right through that observation.
Chancery is also, in its way, a great evader of duties — a system that has learned to sustain itself by never resolving anything.
Skimpole is, if you want to press the reading, the human embodiment of that systemic logic.
A man who perpetually defers, deflects, and consumes the resources of others while producing nothing of substance.
Now, I suspect Edmund would resist that reading as too schematic —
but I would point out that Dickens himself seems to have thought in exactly these structural terms.
I do resist it — but only partly.
Skimpole is too vividly individual to be reduced to an allegory.
The moment you read him purely as a figure for Chancery, you lose what makes him so unnerving — which is that he is recognisably human, recognisably charming, recognisably possible.
Allegories don't make us complicit. Skimpole does.
That, I think, is as fine a note on which to leave Skimpole as any.
Allegories don't make us complicit.
Coming up, we'll be moving from comedy into something more harrowing — the world of Jo, the crossing-sweeper, and what Dickens does with the question of those who fall entirely through the cracks.
Stay with us.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound masterpiece apart, chapter by chapter, idea by idea.

I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be reading one of the most ambitious novels in the English language — a book about justice, identity, and the terrible patience of institutions.
With me today are three extraordinary readers, each bringing a different lens to the text.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has spent a lifetime defending Dickens against what he calls the reductionists — those who would flatten this novel into a political pamphlet.
For Edmund, Bleak House is above all a moral novel — about character, about conscience, about what holds a human being together when the world conspires to undo them.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who has spent years in the archives that Dickens was writing about — the real Court of Chancery, the real Poor Law, the real machinery of Victorian injustice.
James will keep us honest about what the novel is describing — because Dickens wasn't making it up.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted Dickensian who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since — each time, she tells us, finding something new to love and something new to dread.
Caroline reads with her whole heart, and she will make sure we never lose sight of what this novel feels like from the inside.

Today's segment is The Law as Social Machine — the Court of Chancery, what it does to the people caught inside it, and how Dickens turns a legal institution into something approaching a force of nature.
James, you've spent years studying the actual institution Dickens is writing about. Where do we begin?

We begin, I think, where Dickens himself begins — not with a character, not with a plot, but with a description of the Court of Chancery that reads more like a geological survey than an opening chapter.
Dickens opens with fog — that famous, relentless fog — and then draws it inward, into the Court itself.
He writes, in that first chapter:
'This is the Court of Chancery; which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire; which has its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse, and its dead in every churchyard.'
Now, that is not hyperbole — or rather, it is hyperbole in service of something very close to documentary truth.
Chancery suits in the early nineteenth century ran for decades — some for generations.
There are documented cases of litigants who inherited a suit from their fathers and died before it was resolved, leaving it to their children.
The fictional Jarndyce and Jarndyce is outlandish — but only just.
James is quite right to flag the documentary element, and I wouldn't diminish it for a moment.
But what strikes me about that opening chapter is something beyond sociology — it is the sheer rhetorical confidence of the thing.
Dickens constructs Chancery not merely as a failing institution but as a metaphysical condition.
Consider the sentence: 'Suffer any wrong that can be done you, rather than come here.'
'Suffer any wrong that can be done you, rather than come here.'
That injunction is not aimed at the reader as citizen — it is aimed at the reader as a moral agent who must weigh enduring injustice against submitting to a worse one.
Burke would have understood that perfectly — the idea that reform of institutions is necessary, but that the institution, however corrupt, still shapes the character of those within it.
Richard Carstone is the most devastating illustration of that principle in the entire novel.
Richard — yes, I want to come to Richard, because I think he's the character who makes the law feel most like a living thing devouring a person in real time.
But I'd like to dwell a moment on the opening, because I think the texture of that prose is doing something extraordinary.
Dickens gives us that great fog passage — 'Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping.'
'Fog everywhere. Fog up the river... fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping.'
The word 'defiled' stops me every time I read it — because fog doesn't defile, fog is passive, fog is neutral.
But Dickens loads it with moral weight, and suddenly the fog itself feels complicit — the whole environment participates in the corruption.
That's what makes this opening so overwhelming on re-reading — you realize the world of the novel is contaminated before a single character has appeared.
Caroline's point about contamination is important, and I'd extend it historically.
The actual Court of Chancery in the 1820s and 1830s — which is roughly the period Dickens is evoking — was not merely slow.
It was structurally perverse: the fees that kept the lawyers fed were generated by delay, not resolution.
Every adjournment, every procedural motion, every fresh affidavit — all of it produced billable work.
Dickens captures this with the figure of Mr. Vholes — Richard's solicitor — who is one of the most chilling portraits of professional parasitism in English fiction.
Dickens describes him as quietly devouring Richard, inch by inch, with the appearance of perfect respectability.
'The one great principle of the English law is, to make business for itself.'
That line lands differently when you know it isn't satire — it is reportage.
James, I grant you the structural critique entirely — and the Vholes passage is extraordinary.
But I want to insist on something that the purely institutional reading tends to elide.
Richard Carstone is not destroyed by Chancery in the way that a machine destroys a passive object.
Richard has a flaw — a failure of will, an inability to commit to any endeavour that does not promise the great Chancery windfall.
He abandons medicine, he abandons the law, he abandons the army — not because Chancery forces him to, but because he has given his imagination over to it entirely.
John Jarndyce says it precisely — and with great sorrow — when he tells Esther that Richard is the heir of a ruined suit, and that the suit has taken possession of him rather than the reverse.
'It has been in his nature,' Jarndyce says, 'to pursue it... It is the fatal legacy of the case.'
The law is the occasion for Richard's destruction — but the capacity for that destruction was already in him.
That is a moral argument, not a political one — and Dickens is making both simultaneously.
Edmund, I hear you — and I think you're right that Richard has a weakness Dickens traces with tremendous care.
But what moves me — what has always moved me — is that Dickens refuses to let Richard be simply culpable.
There's a moment near the end, when Richard is visibly dying — wasted, hollow — and he says to Esther, 'I have thought better of many things, Esther.'
'I have thought better of many things, Esther. I begin to see that things have gone wrong with me.'
That recognition, that tiny late clarity — it's almost unbearable.
Because it comes too late, and because the system that helped ruin him has no mechanism whatsoever for registering his tragedy.
Chancery doesn't notice. Chancery never notices.
That's what I mean when I say the law in this novel functions as a machine — it processes, it continues, it is utterly indifferent to the human wreckage in its wake.
And the indifference Caroline describes is structural, not incidental — which is the crucial point.
Consider what happens when Jarndyce and Jarndyce finally — finally — reaches a conclusion.
The entire estate has been consumed by legal costs.
Nothing remains for the beneficiaries — nothing at all.
And the court simply — closes the case.
There is no reckoning, no accountability, no acknowledgement that generations of human life have been sacrificed to a procedural void.
Dickens renders this with a kind of deadpan horror — the lawyers gather, someone mentions that costs have absorbed the estate, and then they simply move on to the next matter.
That is what a machine does. It continues.
There's something almost satirical in the resolution — if resolution is even the right word — of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
Edmund, I want to bring you in here — because you've mentioned Esther, and her relationship to all of this is quite different from Richard's.
She exists alongside the case, rather than being consumed by it — and that distinction seems crucial to how Dickens distributes his moral weight.
That is precisely it — and I think Esther's position is Dickens' most carefully considered rebuttal to the law's logic.
Esther Summerson keeps house. She tends to the sick. She maintains.
In a novel saturated with drift and delay and procedural entropy, Esther represents what the law is constitutionally incapable of producing — concrete, embodied care.
Her famous self-deprecations — 'I know I am not clever' — are Dickens doing something rather cunning.
He is insisting that the virtues which hold society together have nothing to do with legal reasoning or institutional cleverness.
They are domestic, immediate, personal — and therefore entirely outside the law's jurisdiction.
Her keys — her literal bunch of household keys, which Jarndyce gives her — are a beautiful counter-image to the seals and writs that govern everyone else's fate.
The keys — yes — I have always loved that detail.
There's a wonderful moment where Esther says she felt that day something new begin — a quiet sense of responsibility, almost domestic joy.
And then she immediately undercuts it — 'I am not the heroine of this story, if it has one.'
'I am not the heroine of this story, if it has one.'
That 'if it has one' is doing so much work — it's Dickens acknowledging that his novel has no tidy moral arc, that the story resists the shape of heroism.
The law has no hero either, of course — only process and precedent.
And so Esther, who claims not to be a heroine, becomes the closest thing this novel has to one — precisely by refusing the systems of recognition that the law relies on.
I'd add one more figure to this conversation — one who is entirely outside the law's notice, and whose exclusion is Dickens' most damning indictment of the whole system.
Jo, the crossing-sweeper.
Jo cannot read. Jo has no name that the law would recognise. Jo has no address, no parish, no legal existence whatsoever.

And yet the law touches him — repeatedly, brutally — through the figure of the beadle, through 'moving on,' through every mechanism of official power that exists not to protect him but to erase him from view.
Dickens' great apostrophe to Jo — 'Dead, your Majesty' — is one of the most politically charged sentences in Victorian fiction.
'Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right reverends and wrong reverends of every order.'
The roll call of authority — Majesty, Lords, reverends — all of them named precisely to be arraigned.
Jo doesn't know the law exists. But the law knows exactly how to be rid of him.
Jo's death — and that extraordinary passage — will come back to haunt us later in the series.
But I think you've given us something essential here — the law in Bleak House is not simply a target of satire.
It is a world — with its own weather, its own ecology, its own indifferent metabolism.
And the people inside it — Richard, Jo, even the Lord Chancellor himself, buried in his paper — are subject to forces larger than their individual choices.

In our next segment, we turn to one of Dickens' greatest formal innovations — the doubled narrative, and what it means that this novel tells its story in two different voices, from two irreconcilable perspectives.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Threads Converge: Meaning in Dickens' Labyrinth

utterances.text: We've spent this episode moving through what feels like an endless labyrinth — Chancery, fog, Chesney Wold, the brickmakers' hovels, the Inns of Court.
But Dickens, of course, is not building a maze to lose us in.
He is building one to show us how the threads connect — and what it costs to follow them.
So for this final conversation, I want to ask each of you: what is Bleak House ultimately about?
What does the novel's vast, intricate architecture finally mean?
Edmund, you've spent a lifetime with Dickens — I'd like to start with you.
It is a novel about responsibility — specifically, about what happens when human beings abdicate it.
Chancery, the fog, the interminable suit — these are expressions of collective abdication dressed in legal costume.
But Dickens does not leave us there, and this is where I think some readings go badly wrong.
Against that vast systemic failure, he places individual acts of grace — and he insists they matter.
Think of Jarndyce quietly withdrawing from his suit at the end — no fanfare, no speech.
He simply refuses to be consumed by the thing that has consumed everyone else.
Dickens frames that as heroism — understated, English, moral heroism.
Burke would have recognised it: not the grand gesture, but the quiet performance of duty.
I agree with Edmund about Jarndyce — genuinely — but I want to press further into what Esther's chapters do.
Because Esther is not simply a counter-example to the fog.
She is herself a kind of question the novel is asking: can a person build a self when the world has refused to acknowledge she has one?
There is that devastating line early in her narrative, where she confides to her doll as a child — her only confidante.
"I was to no one upon earth what Dolly was to me."
That sentence breaks something open in me every single time.
It tells you what Esther is building against — absolute emotional isolation from birth.
And yet she becomes — of all the characters in the novel — the most generous reader of other people.
That is Dickens' great, quiet argument: that character can be earned, even when it is never given.
Both of those readings are true — and I don't want to dispute them — but I keep returning to what the novel does structurally.
Dickens chose to write a novel with two narrators: Esther's first-person account, and the anonymous third-person omniscient voice.
That is not a small formal decision — it is the argument of the book made architectural.
The omniscient narrator sees the system — sees how Chancery grinds, how Parliament postures, how the fog spreads.
Esther sees the individual — one face at a time, one relationship at a time.
Neither perspective alone is sufficient.
Together, they enact Dickens' real claim: you cannot understand injustice without seeing both its machinery and its human cost.
And the novel earns that claim because Dickens spent two years making sure both registers are equally vivid.
James, I'll grant you the formal argument — it's well made.
Though I'd note that Johnson warned us, long before Dickens, that any artist who wishes to move must first instruct.
Dickens knows this — which is why the novel's closing image is not of Chancery dissolved, or Parliament reformed.
It is of Esther settled at a new Bleak House, with Allan Woodcourt, with her children — with a life built.
Some have found that conclusion unsatisfying — too domestic, too tidy.
I find it the most honest thing Dickens ever wrote.
Because institutions rarely reform — but people, sometimes, manage to live well despite them.
I want to come back to something that hasn't been said yet — which is the novel's very last paragraph.
Esther breaks off mid-sentence, almost mid-thought, as though she cannot quite believe she is permitted to be happy.
She says Allan has told her she is prettier than she ever was — and she stops there.
"I know that I am prettier than I ever was. I did not know that I was prettier than I ever was. I have been told so. But I must write it, perhaps, because I want everyone to know it."
The hesitation, the self-correction — that is not sentimentality.
That is a woman who has spent her whole life being told she has no right to exist — finally, tentatively, claiming a small beauty.
It devastates me, even now.
And there, of course, is the thread that binds the whole novel together.
Jo dies in Chapter Forty-Seven — barely knowing his own name, unable to read the placard that says 'move on.'
The omniscient narrator interrupts the scene with one of the great sustained passages of moral fury in English literature.

"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order. Dead, men and women, born with Heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us, every day."
That is Dickens stepping entirely outside the frame of fiction to accuse.
Not Chancery. Not a system. Us.
And then, without a breath, the novel goes on — because it must, because life does.
But Dickens has made sure we cannot read the pages that follow without feeling what we just heard.
Jo's death — that passage — is, I think, the hinge on which the whole novel turns.
Edmund, you said Dickens insists individual acts of grace matter — but does he also insist that they are enough?
Or is that charge — 'and dying thus around us, every day' — a demand for something more?
He is a Victorian Christian — he would say they are necessary, not sufficient.
What he will not do — and this is his great discipline — is tell us precisely what institutional reform looks like.
He is a novelist, not a legislator.
His job is to make us feel the cost of the status quo — and then leave us, as citizens, to do the rest.
And perhaps that is why, after nearly two hundred years, we are still doing this — sitting around a table and arguing about it.
Because Bleak House refuses to resolve itself into a lesson.
It stays alive, the way only the great novels do — as a question that keeps asking itself back.
And every generation reads it through its own fog.
Every generation reads it through its own fog — I think we'll leave it there.
Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you.
You've made the labyrinth feel navigable — which is, I suspect, exactly what Dickens wanted.
For Bleak House Unpacked, I'm your host — thank you for listening, and thank you for caring about books this much.
The fog, as Dickens reminds us, is always somewhere — but so, thank God, are the people who refuse to let it have the last word.

London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.

misty clouds.

Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on. This scarecrow of a suit has, in
course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it
means. The parties to it understand it least, but it has been
observed that no two Chancery lawyers can talk about it for five
minutes without coming to a total disagreement as to all the
premises. Innumerable children have been born into the cause;
innumerable young people have married into it; innumerable old people
have died out of it. Scores of persons have deliriously found
themselves made parties in Jarndyce and Jarndyce without knowing how
or why; whole families have inherited legendary hatreds with the
suit. The little plaintiff or defendant who was promised a new
rocking-horse when Jarndyce and Jarndyce should be settled has grown
up, possessed himself of a real horse, and trotted away into the
other world. Fair wards of court have faded into mothers and
grandmothers; a long procession of Chancellors has come in and gone
out; the legion of bills in the suit have been transformed into mere
bills of mortality; there are not three Jarndyces left upon the earth
perhaps since old Tom Jarndyce in despair blew his brains out at a
coffee-house in Chancery Lane; but Jarndyce and Jarndyce still drags
its dreary length before the court, perennially hopeless.

“There again!” said Mr. Gridley with no diminution of his rage. “The
system! I am told on all hands, it’s the system. I mustn’t look to
individuals. It’s the system. I mustn’t go into court and say, ‘My
Lord, I beg to know this from you—is this right or wrong? Have you
the face to tell me I have received justice and therefore am
dismissed?’ My Lord knows nothing of it. He sits there to administer
the system. I mustn’t go to Mr. Tulkinghorn, the solicitor in
Lincoln’s Inn Fields, and say to him when he makes me furious by
being so cool and satisfied—as they all do, for I know they gain by
it while I lose, don’t I?—I mustn’t say to him, ‘I will have
something out of some one for my ruin, by fair means or foul!’ HE is
not responsible. It’s the system. But, if I do no violence to any of
them, here—I may! I don’t know what may happen if I am carried
beyond myself at last! I will accuse the individual workers of that
system against me, face to face, before the great eternal bar!”
c15:p111.summary: Gridley criticizes how he is told to blame 'the system' rather than individuals, but he maintains his right to hold the individual workers accountable, threatening them with judgment.

c1:p6.text:
Who happen to be in the Lord Chancellor’s court this murky afternoon
besides the Lord Chancellor, the counsel in the cause, two or three
counsel who are never in any cause, and the well of solicitors before
mentioned? There is the registrar below the judge, in wig and gown;
and there are two or three maces, or petty-bags, or privy purses, or
whatever they may be, in legal court suits. These are all yawning,
for no crumb of amusement ever falls from Jarndyce and Jarndyce (the
cause in hand), which was squeezed dry years upon years ago. The
short-hand writers, the reporters of the court, and the reporters of
the newspapers invariably decamp with the rest of the regulars when
Jarndyce and Jarndyce comes on. Their places are a blank. Standing on
a seat at the side of the hall, the better to peer into the curtained
sanctuary, is a little mad old woman in a squeezed bonnet who is
always in court, from its sitting to its rising, and always expecting
some incomprehensible judgment to be given in her favour. Some say
she really is, or was, a party to a suit, but no one knows for
certain because no one cares. She carries some small litter in a
reticule which she calls her documents, principally consisting of
paper matches and dry lavender. A sallow prisoner has come up, in
custody, for the half-dozenth time to make a personal application “to
purge himself of his contempt,” which, being a solitary surviving
executor who has fallen into a state of conglomeration about accounts
of which it is not pretended that he had ever any knowledge, he is
not at all likely ever to do. In the meantime his prospects in life
are ended. Another ruined suitor, who periodically appears from
Shropshire and breaks out into efforts to address the Chancellor at
the close of the day’s business and who can by no means be made to
understand that the Chancellor is legally ignorant of his existence
after making it desolate for a quarter of a century, plants himself
in a good place and keeps an eye on the judge, ready to call out “My
Lord!” in a voice of sonorous complaint on the instant of his rising.
A few lawyers’ clerks and others who know this suitor by sight linger
on the chance of his furnishing some fun and enlivening the dismal
weather a little.
c1:p6.summary: The court contains a miscellany of tragic figures: a mad woman with paper-match 'documents,' a prisoner repeatedly attempting to clear contempt charges, and a ruined suitor from Shropshire who periodically appears to plead to an indifferent Chancellor.

finger—“Your mother, Esther, is your disgrace, and you were hers.

better and will feel it too, as no one save a woman can. I have
forgiven her”—but her face did not relent—“the wrong she did to me,
and I say no more of it, though it was greater than you will ever
know—than any one will ever know but I, the sufferer. For yourself,
unfortunate girl, orphaned and degraded from the first of these evil

c15:p109.text:
“Mr. Jarndyce,” he said, “consider my case. As true as there is a
heaven above us, this is my case. I am one of two brothers. My father
(a farmer) made a will and left his farm and stock and so forth to my
mother for her life. After my mother’s death, all was to come to me
except a legacy of three hundred pounds that I was then to pay my
brother. My mother died. My brother some time afterwards claimed his
legacy. I and some of my relations said that he had had a part of it
already in board and lodging and some other things. Now mind! That
was the question, and nothing else. No one disputed the will; no one
disputed anything but whether part of that three hundred pounds had
been already paid or not. To settle that question, my brother filing
a bill, I was obliged to go into this accursed Chancery; I was forced
there because the law forced me and would let me go nowhere else.
Seventeen people were made defendants to that simple suit! It first
came on after two years. It was then stopped for another two years
while the master (may his head rot off!) inquired whether I was my
father’s son, about which there was no dispute at all with any mortal
creature. He then found out that there were not defendants
enough—remember, there were only seventeen as yet!—but that we must
have another who had been left out and must begin all over again. The
costs at that time—before the thing was begun!—were three times the
legacy. My brother would have given up the legacy, and joyful, to
escape more costs. My whole estate, left to me in that will of my
father’s, has gone in costs. The suit, still undecided, has fallen
into rack, and ruin, and despair, with everything else—and here I
stand, this day! Now, Mr. Jarndyce, in your suit there are thousands
and thousands involved, where in mine there are hundreds. Is mine
less hard to bear or is it harder to bear, when my whole living was
in it and has been thus shamefully sucked away?”

c1:p5.text:
On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be
sitting here—as here he is—with a foggy glory round his head,
softly fenced in with crimson cloth and curtains, addressed by a
large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an
interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain
and breaks the heart, that there is not an honourable man among its
practitioners who would not give—who does not often give—the
warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come
here!”
c1:p5.summary: An extended satirical tableau of the Lord Chancellor and court staff in their fog-wrapped surroundings, processing endless technicalities while suitors are ruined financially and psychologically; Chancery has destroyed lives across the nation.

seen, and that they can very well do without much beauty in me—even
 supposing—.
c67:p27.summary: Esther declines to judge her own beauty but celebrates the beauty and goodness of her family members, finding completeness in their worth.
c67:p27.best_quote: But I know that my dearest little pets are very pretty, and that my darling is very beautiful, and that my husband is very handsome, and that my guardian has the brightest and most benevolent face that ever was seen.
